On the last day of the municipal pool, somebody stole the clock. They left the screws in a neat pile on the lifeguard’s chair. At ten past nine, according to my phone, my mother stood beneath the pale circle on the wall and said, “Good. Now nobody can tell me my break is over.”

She’d been retired for eleven years.

I had agreed to record the building before they tore it down. This was my idea, though by then I’d explained it to so many people that I’d come to resent whoever had thought of it. The city archivist wanted dates, names, and a brief account of the roof repairs. I wanted the sound of a bare foot slapping a wet tile. Each of us thought the other was missing the point.

My mother brought a grocery bag containing her old whistle, two egg sandwiches, and a padlock whose combination she’d forgotten. She rattled the padlock at me.

“You used to open this.”

“Thirty-six, ten, twenty-two.”

She spun the dial. It opened.

“Why have you got room for that in your head?”

“I don’t get to choose.”

“Apparently not,” she said, and put it back in the bag.

The pool had closed to swimmers in August. Now it was November, and the only water left was a green puddle over the drain in the deep end. A beach ball lay down there, soft on one side. The blue lane markings looked freshly painted. From the edge you could see a hairline crack running through all six lanes, as if somebody had tried to fold the pool in half.

I put a microphone on a stand and asked my mother to walk from the changing rooms to the shallow end. She took off her shoes. Halfway across, she stopped and picked up a hairpin.

“Keep going,” I said.

“You want somebody to step on this?”

There was nobody else in the building. I started to say so, then watched her carry the hairpin to a trash can that had no liner. It made a sound like a coin dropped into a well. I’d already stopped recording.

We tried the whistle next. She gave it one short blast, and a pigeon came out of a hole in the ceiling. Neither of us had known it was there. It flew the length of the pool twice before finding the open door, and my mother laughed so hard she had to sit down.

“Did you get that?” she asked.

I had, but the whistle had overloaded the microphone. On playback it sounded as though somebody had torn a piece of paper close to my ear.

During lunch my mother told me about a woman who had come every Tuesday for nine years and never got in the water. She sat on the lowest bleacher in a purple bathing cap and read the newspaper. When the woman stopped coming, my mother called the number on her membership form. The woman answered on the second ring. She’d started taking an upholstery class. She had a chair at home that needed doing.

“What did you say?” I asked.

“I asked her what color.”

“What color?”

“Oh, I don’t know,” my mother said. She pinched a strip of egg white out of her sandwich and ate it. “I only remember how relieved I was when she picked up.”

After lunch we went to the changing rooms. The locker doors were different enough that I recorded six of them, then felt sorry for the seventh and recorded that too. My mother sat on the wooden bench and turned the padlock dial back and forth. She had taught me to swim in this building, but not during her shift. After closing, she’d get in up to her shoulders and hold a nickel flat on her palm, just below the surface. If I put my face in, I could have it. I must have made two dollars that summer, all of it from the same nickel. I kept forgetting to take it out of my swimsuit, and she kept finding it in the washing machine.

“Would you talk about teaching me to swim?” I asked.

She looked at the microphone. “You never liked to get your ears wet.”

“Right.”

“You’d get your whole head under, then come up with one ear still dry. I wish I knew how you did that.”

I waited for more. She turned the dial again.

At four, the man from Public Works arrived to lock up. It turned out he had taken the clock. His daughter had learned to tell time by it while waiting for her brother’s swimming lessons to end. He’d put it in his truck, then worried all day that he ought to have asked somebody. My mother told him that if anyone wanted it back, he should say she’d taken it.

“You don’t work here anymore,” he said.

“That’s why it’ll take them a while to find me.”

He gave us five minutes. I went back for the microphone stand and found my mother on the lifeguard’s chair, putting on her shoes. Without the clock above her, I could see where somebody had tested three shades of blue on the wall and painted over only two of them.

“Want a hand?” I asked.

“In a minute,” she said. “I’ve got a stone in here.”

She shook her shoe into her palm. I had my headphones on, and I could hear the little knocks she gave the heel, the laces brushing the metal chair, the man out in the lobby trying one key and then another. I could hear myself breathing. I held still while she checked the other shoe.

Months later, the archivist asked me to identify a voice on the recording. I put on my headphones. There was my mother saying *In a minute*, but that wasn’t the part he meant. He meant the voice after hers, so low I had to turn it up. It was me. I said *Okay*.

I almost wrote back that it was nobody. Then I gave him my name.
